title: Model Versioning
shortDefinition: The practice of systematically tracking and managing different versions of an AI model over time.
definition: Model versioning is the practice of systematically tracking and managing different versions of an AI model as it's trained, updated, and deployed over time — recording exactly which data, code, and configuration produced each version, enabling safe rollback if a new version underperforms, and ensuring reproducibility for audit or debugging purposes. Without proper versioning, teams can lose track of exactly what's running in production or why a model's behavior changed between updates.

sections.title: Why model versioning matters for production reliability
sections.description: Without systematic versioning, teams risk being unable to roll back or audit model behavior.

content.text: Without systematic versioning, a team deploying a new model version risks not being able to quickly and confidently roll back if the new version underperforms in ways that weren't caught during testing — a real risk since production behavior can sometimes differ from validation results in subtle ways. Versioning also supports auditability: when a model's behavior is questioned (a bias complaint, an unexpected decision), you need to know exactly which version was running, what data trained it, and what configuration was active at that time, which is impossible to reconstruct reliably without disciplined version tracking.

items: Safe rollback — revert to known-good version if new version underperforms.
Auditability — know exactly which version was running at any time.
Reproducibility — recreate any version for debugging or validation.
Production confidence — deploy updates knowing rollback is possible.
Incident investigation — trace behavior changes to specific versions.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Without versioning, rolling back to a known-good previous state becomes difficult or impossible, potentially extending production problems far longer than necessary.

Comprehensive model versioning records the specific training data version used, the code and hyperparameter configuration for that training run, the resulting model artifact itself, validation performance metrics for that specific version, and deployment history (when each version went live and when it was retired or rolled back). Tools like MLflow provide a model registry specifically designed to track this information systematically, rather than relying on informal naming conventions or scattered documentation that becomes unreliable over time.

items: Training data version — exactly which data was used.
Code and hyperparameters — configuration for the training run.
Model artifact — the trained model file itself.
Validation metrics — performance data for each version.
Deployment history — when each version went live and was retired.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of model versioning

content.text: Model versioning has limitations. It requires discipline to maintain consistently, and historical tracking is only as complete as what was recorded. Versioning infrastructure adds operational overhead, and teams can still deploy the wrong version without proper deployment controls. Versioning alone doesn't prevent model quality issues — it only helps manage them once they occur. Performance metrics may not capture all aspects of model behavior, and versioning doesn't address data versioning or pipeline dependencies.

items: Discipline requirement — versioning only works if consistently used.
Historical gaps — only captures what was recorded at the time.
Operational overhead — adds infrastructure management burden.
Deployment controls — versioning alone doesn't prevent wrong deployments.
Quality issues — versioning helps manage issues, not prevent them.
Limited metrics — performance metrics may not capture all behavior.

content.title: Important
content.text: Model versioning is essential for production reliability, but it's only one part of MLOps infrastructure — it must be combined with deployment controls and monitoring.

sections.title: Best practices for model versioning implementation

content.text: Implementing effective model versioning requires systematic tracking, clear procedures, and team discipline. The following practices can help ensure your versioning infrastructure delivers real value.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Use a model registry (MLflow, Weights & Biases, or similar) from day one.
Track training data version, code, hyperparameters, and metrics for every version.
Establish clear version naming and deployment procedures.
Document rollback procedures before they're needed.
Integrate versioning with deployment pipelines.
Store model artifacts in a secure, accessible location.
Audit versioning compliance regularly.
Include versioning in model development checklists.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure deployment rollback time — versioning's value is measured by how quickly you can revert to a known-good state when something goes wrong.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about model versioning

items.question: What happens if we don't have proper model versioning and a new version causes problems?
items.answer: Without versioning, rolling back to a known-good previous state becomes difficult or impossible, potentially extending the duration of a production problem significantly longer than necessary.

items.question: What is a model registry?
items.answer: A model registry (like the one built into MLflow) is a centralized system for storing, tracking, and managing different versions of a model, including their associated metadata, performance metrics, and deployment status.

items.question: Does model versioning slow down our ability to deploy updates quickly?
items.answer: Properly implemented versioning is designed to support fast, confident deployment — knowing you can roll back safely if needed actually enables faster iteration, not slower.

items.question: Can versioning help us understand why a model's behavior changed over time?
items.answer: Yes, this is one of its primary benefits — comparing the training data and configuration between versions helps diagnose unexpected behavior changes.

items.question: How long does setting up model versioning infrastructure take?
items.answer: 6–14 weeks depending on whether it's new infrastructure or retroactively establishing tracking for existing models.

items.question: Is model versioning relevant for LLM-based applications, not just custom-trained models?
items.answer: Yes, in a different form — tracking prompt versions, RAG knowledge base versions, and model provider/version selections similarly benefits from systematic version tracking, even without traditional model training.

items.question: What is the difference between model versioning and experiment tracking?
items.answer: Experiment tracking records training runs during development (including many failed or experimental runs). Model versioning tracks the subset of models that are promoted to production or considered for production. Experiment tracking is for research; model versioning is for production.

items.question: What information should be stored with each model version?
items.answer: Each version should store: model artifact, training data version, code version, hyperparameters, validation metrics, training timestamp, and deployment status. This ensures full reproducibility and auditability.

items.question: How do you handle versioning for retrained models?
items.answer: Each retraining run creates a new model version with new training data, updated metrics, and a new timestamp. The versioning system tracks the lineage — which model version was retrained and why.

items.question: Can versioning help with A/B testing of models?
items.answer: Yes — versioning provides the infrastructure for A/B testing different model versions in production. You can deploy multiple versions simultaneously and compare their performance before deciding which to promote.
